population: 1,192 genotyped members of the Iowa 65+ Rural Health Study, European ancestry, enrolled at age 65 or over; genotype counts C/C 940, T/C 239, T/T 10
conclusion: Table 2 and Figure 1. Adjusted for sex, BMI, smoking, alcohol consumption, comorbidity count and a BMI-by-smoking interaction. T/T adjusted mean age at death was 5.5 y below C/C and 5.9 y below T/C (q=0.012); crude means 82.1 y (T/T), 87.6 y (C/C), 88.0 y (T/C). Rests on 10 T/T individuals. population: 169 long-lived inhabitants of Bama County, Guangxi, China aged 90-110 y and 158 healthy internal controls aged 26-82 y from the same region
conclusion: Table 4. C allele 97/338 (28.7%) in the long-lived and 85/306 (27.8%) in the internal controls: no difference. This is the better-matched of the paper's two comparisons, both groups being drawn from the same longevity-enriched region, and it is null.

population: 169 long-lived inhabitants of Bama County, Guangxi, China aged 90-110 y and 176 healthy external controls aged 20-82 y without a family history of exceptional longevity
conclusion: Table 4. C allele 97/338 (28.7%) in the long-lived and 136/352 (38.6%) in the external controls, OR 0.639: the C allele is LOWER in the long-lived. This is the opposite sign to the paper's stated conclusion that the C allele is associated with longevity, and it is the sign that PMID 41249831 reproduces incorrectly. The two control groups also differ from each other (27.8% vs 38.6%, p=0.003), so this contrast most likely reflects control selection rather than longevity.
statistical_test: Pearson chi-square, allelic; multinomial logistic regression
